topics.name: Nature of Matter
topics.summary: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. It is broadly classified into pure substances (fixed composition) and mixtures (variable composition). Pure substances split further into elements (one kind of atom, cannot be simplified chemically, e.g. Na, O2) and compounds (two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio, e.g. H2O, NaCl). Mixtures are either homogeneous (uniform composition throughout, e.g. sugar solution, brass, air) or heterogeneous (visibly non-uniform, e.g. sand in water). Physical properties (colour, density, melting point) can be measured without changing composition; chemical properties (reactivity, combustibility) describe how a substance transforms into new substances.
topics.worked_example: Classify brass: it is made of Cu and Zn atoms mixed in a variable ratio with uniform composition throughout → it is a homogeneous mixture (an alloy), not a compound, because its Cu:Zn ratio is not chemically fixed.
common_mistakes: Calling an alloy (brass, steel) a compound just because it "looks" like one substance
Assuming all mixtures are heterogeneous and visibly separable
Forgetting that a solution (e.g. salt water) is still a mixture, not a compound

topics.name: Measurement and Significant Figures
topics.summary: Chemistry uses the SI system of units (kilogram for mass, mole for amount of substance, kelvin for temperature, etc.). Every measurement carries some uncertainty, expressed through significant figures: all certain digits plus one estimated digit. Rules: non-zero digits are always significant; zeros between non-zero digits are significant; leading zeros are never significant; trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant. In addition/subtraction, the result keeps as many decimal places as the least precise number. In multiplication/division, the result keeps as many significant figures as the factor with the fewest. Large or small numbers are conveniently written in scientific notation, N × 10n, with exactly one non-zero digit before the decimal point.
key_formulas: Addition/subtraction: match the fewest decimal places
Multiplication/division: match the fewest significant figures
topics.worked_example: 4.70 cm × 2.5 cm = 11.75 cm2 on a calculator, but since 2.5 cm has only 2 significant figures, the answer must be rounded to 2 significant figures: 12 cm2.
common_mistakes: Reporting every digit a calculator displays, ignoring the least precise input
Treating leading zeros in 0.0025 as significant (only 2 and 5 count)
Forgetting that the exponent in scientific notation (10<sup>n</sup>) never adds to the significant figure count

topics.name: Laws of Chemical Combination
topics.summary: Several 18th/19th-century laws describe how elements combine. The law of conservation of mass (Lavoisier): mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. The law of definite (constant) proportions (Proust): a pure compound always contains the same elements combined in the same fixed mass ratio, regardless of its source. The law of multiple proportions (Dalton): when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are always in a ratio of small whole numbers (e.g. O in CO and CO2 is in ratio 1:2). Gay Lussac's law of gaseous volumes: gases react in volumes that are in a simple whole-number ratio to each other and to the product volumes, at the same temperature and pressure.
topics.worked_example: Carbon forms CO (12 g C : 16 g O) and CO2 (12 g C : 32 g O). For the same fixed mass of carbon (12 g), the oxygen masses 16 g and 32 g are in the simple ratio 1:2 — the law of multiple proportions.
common_mistakes: Confusing the law of definite proportions (one compound, fixed ratio) with the law of multiple proportions (two+ compounds, ratio between ratios)
Forgetting that Gay Lussac's law applies to gas volumes only, at the same T and P
Assuming conservation of mass means reactant and product masses must look "equal" per substance, rather than in total

topics.name: Dalton's Atomic Theory
topics.summary: John Dalton (1808) proposed that: (1) matter consists of indivisible atoms; (2) atoms of a given element are identical in mass and properties; (3) atoms of different elements differ in mass and properties; (4) compounds form when atoms of different elements combine in simple whole-number ratios; (5) atoms can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction (explaining conservation of mass). The theory successfully explained the laws of definite and multiple proportions, but later discoveries required modification: atoms are divisible into subatomic particles, and isotopes show that atoms of the same element can have different masses. Avogadro's later distinction between atoms and molecules also resolved gas-volume observations Dalton's theory alone could not explain.
topics.worked_example: Dalton's theory explains why water always has an H:O mass ratio of 1:8, since water "atoms" (molecules) always contain the same fixed combination of H and O atoms.
common_mistakes: Treating Dalton's postulates as still 100% accurate today without noting later modifications (isotopes, subatomic particles)
Forgetting that Avogadro's atom/molecule distinction, not Dalton's theory alone, explains simple whole-number gas volume ratios
Mixing up which postulate explains which law (identical atoms → definite proportions; simple ratios → multiple proportions)

topics.name: Atomic Mass
topics.summary: The modern atomic mass scale is based on the carbon-12 standard: 1 atomic mass unit (amu or u) = 1/12th the mass of one 12C atom ≈ 1.66 × 10−24 g. Since most elements exist as a mixture of isotopes with different natural abundances, the value listed on the periodic table is the average atomic mass: a weighted average using each isotope's mass and its percentage (or fractional) abundance. If an element has isotopes of mass m1 and m2 with abundances (as decimals) x1 and x2 (x1 + x2 = 1), average atomic mass = m1x1 + m2x2. This weighted-average equation can also be solved backward to find an unknown abundance if the average atomic mass is given.
key_formulas: Average atomic mass = Σ (isotope mass × fractional abundance)
common_mistakes: Taking a simple (unweighted) average of the isotope masses instead of weighting by abundance
Forgetting that abundances must add up to 100% (or 1) when solving for an unknown abundance
Confusing mass number (a whole number, protons + neutrons) with the element's average atomic mass (a decimal)

topics.name: Molecular Mass and Formula Mass
topics.summary: Molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms present in one molecule of a covalent substance (e.g. H2O = 2(1) + 16 = 18). For ionic compounds, which exist as an extended lattice rather than discrete molecules, the equivalent quantity is called the formula mass (e.g. NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5), calculated the same way from the formula unit. Both are usually expressed in amu (per particle) or as the numerically equal molar mass in g mol−1 (per mole). Hydrated salts (e.g. CuSO4·5H2O) include the mass of their water of crystallisation in the total formula mass.
key_formulas: Molecular/formula mass = Σ (atomic mass × number of atoms of each element in the formula)
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply an atom's mass by its subscript (e.g. using one O instead of four in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>)
Calling an ionic compound's formula mass a "molecular mass" (technically incorrect, since no discrete molecule exists)
Leaving out the water of crystallisation's mass when calculating a hydrate's total formula mass

topics.name: Mole Concept and Molar Mass
topics.summary: The mole is the SI unit for amount of substance: 1 mole of any entity (atoms, molecules, ions) contains exactly Avogadro's number, NA = 6.022 × 1023, of that entity. Molar mass is the mass in grams of one mole of a substance, numerically equal to its atomic/molecular/formula mass in amu. The three core conversions are: moles = mass ÷ molar mass; number of particles = moles × NA; and, for gases at STP (0°C, 1 atm), volume = moles × 22.4 L mol−1. These relationships form the computational backbone for almost every other topic in this chapter.
key_formulas: Volume at STP = moles × 22.4 L mol<sup>−1</sup>
topics.worked_example: Moles in 9 g of water (molar mass 18): 9 ÷ 18 = 0.5 mol, containing 0.5 × 6.022 × 1023 = 3.011 × 1023 molecules.
common_mistakes: Inverting the mass/molar mass division (computing molar mass ÷ mass instead)
Forgetting to convert a gas volume from millilitres to litres before dividing by 22.4 L mol<sup>−1</sup>
Multiplying by N<sub>A</sub> without first converting the given quantity into moles

topics.name: Percentage Composition
topics.summary: Percentage composition expresses what fraction, by mass, of a compound's total molar mass comes from each constituent element: %element = (mass of that element in one mole of compound ÷ molar mass of compound) × 100. It is found either theoretically (from a known formula) or experimentally (from combustion/gravimetric analysis), and the experimental value is used to work out a compound's empirical formula. Percentage composition also underlies everyday quantities such as the nitrogen content of a fertiliser or the mass percentage of solute in a solution.
key_formulas: % element = (mass of element in 1 mole of compound / molar mass of compound) × 100
common_mistakes: Dividing by the mass of just one atom of the element instead of the element's total contribution (all atoms of it in the formula)
Forgetting to multiply the final fraction by 100
Confusing an element's percentage with 100% minus a different element's percentage without recalculating

topics.name: Empirical and Molecular Formula
topics.summary: The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound; the molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms in one molecule, and is always a whole-number multiple, n, of the empirical formula: molecular formula = n × (empirical formula), where n = molecular mass ÷ empirical formula mass. To find an empirical formula from percentage composition: convert each percentage to moles (divide by atomic mass), then divide every value by the smallest one to get the simplest ratio. Combustion analysis of organic compounds (measuring CO2 and H2O produced) is a classic experimental route to the empirical formula of hydrocarbons.
key_formulas: n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass
topics.worked_example: Empirical formula CH2O (mass 30), molecular mass 180: n = 180/30 = 6, so molecular formula = (CH2O)6 = C6H12O6.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the empirical formula when the molecular formula was actually asked for (forgetting to multiply by n)
Not fully simplifying the mole ratio to its lowest whole-number terms
In combustion analysis, forgetting that each mole of CO<sub>2</sub> gives 1 mole of C but each mole of H<sub>2</sub>O gives 2 moles of H

topics.name: Stoichiometry
topics.summary: Stoichiometry is the calculation of quantitative (mole and mass) relationships between reactants and products in a balanced chemical equation. The coefficients of a balanced equation give the exact mole ratio in which substances react and form; to convert to mass, first convert the given mass to moles, apply the mole ratio from the equation, then convert back to mass (or volume, using 22.4 L mol−1 at STP for gases). Multi-step problems chain two or more reactions together, carrying the mole count (not the mass) through each step, and only converting to mass at the very end. Balancing itself rests on the law of conservation of mass: atoms of each element must be equal on both sides.
key_formulas: Moles of product = moles of given reactant × (coefficient of product / coefficient of reactant)
topics.worked_example: For N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, moles of NH3 from 6 mol H2: 6 × (2/3) = 4 mol.
common_mistakes: Assuming a 1:1 mole ratio between reactant and product instead of reading the actual balanced coefficients
Converting mass to mass directly, skipping the essential intermediate step of moles
In multi-step problems, converting to mass after the first step instead of carrying moles through every step

topics.name: Limiting Reagent
topics.summary: When reactants are not supplied in the exact mole ratio a balanced equation requires, one reactant runs out first: this is the limiting reagent, and it alone determines the maximum (theoretical) amount of product that can form. Whatever remains of the other reactant(s) once the limiting reagent is exhausted is the excess reagent. To identify the limiting reagent: convert every reactant's given amount to moles, then compare the mole ratio available against the ratio the equation requires (dividing available moles by the equation's coefficient for each reactant is a reliable shortcut — the smallest result identifies the limiting reagent). All product calculations must then be based only on the limiting reagent. Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100 compares what was actually obtained in practice to this theoretical maximum.
key_formulas: Compare (moles available / coefficient) for each reactant — the smallest ratio is limiting
topics.worked_example: For N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, with 1 mol N2 and 2 mol H2: N2 needs 3 mol H2 but only 2 mol is available, so H2 is limiting, and moles NH3 = 2 × (2/3) = 1.33 mol.
common_mistakes: Assuming the reactant with the smaller given mass (rather than the smaller mole-to-coefficient ratio) is automatically limiting
Basing product calculations on the excess reagent instead of the limiting reagent
Forgetting to subtract the amount of excess reagent actually consumed when asked how much is "left over"

topics.name: Concentration of Solutions
topics.summary: Several interrelated terms describe how concentrated a solution is. Molarity (M) = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution in litres (temperature-dependent, since volume changes slightly with temperature). Molality (m) = moles of solute ÷ mass of solvent in kilograms (temperature-independent). Mole fraction (x) = moles of one component ÷ total moles of all components. Mass percentage = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100, and needs the solution's density to convert between mass and volume. Dilution follows M1V1 = M2V2, since the moles of solute stay constant while only the volume changes. When two solutions of the same solute are mixed, total moles and total volumes are simply added (assuming additive volumes) to find the new molarity.
key_formulas: Molarity = moles of solute / volume of solution (L)
Molality = moles of solute / mass of solvent (kg)
Mole fraction = moles of component / total moles
topics.worked_example: Diluting 50 mL of 4 M HCl to 200 mL: M1V1 = M2V2 → 4 × 50 = M2 × 200 → M2 = 1 M.
common_mistakes: Using solvent volume/mass for molarity instead of the total solution volume
Forgetting to include the solution's density when converting between mass percentage and molarity
Averaging two solutions' molarities directly instead of properly weighting by their respective volumes
